Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

This API manages calendar bookings: creating, updating, listing, and canceling appointments across one or more calendars. It handles the scheduling logic itself, including conflict checks, time zone conversion, and recurrence rules, so a client app does not have to reimplement them.

Every booking belongs to a calendar and has a start time, an end time, and a status: `pending`, `confirmed`, or `canceled`. Endpoints accept and return timestamps in ISO 8601 with an explicit offset. The API rejects a request that would double-book a calendar unless the client sets `allow_overlap` to true.

Authentication uses a bearer token scoped to one account. Each account can own multiple calendars, and each calendar can have its own list of collaborators with read or write access. Rate limits apply per token: 60 requests per minute for reads, 20 per minute for writes.

The guide covers the following, in order: authentication and token scopes, calendar and booking resource shapes, the endpoints for creating and querying bookings, recurrence and exception handling, webhook notifications for booking changes, and error codes with retry guidance.

Read the authentication section first. Every other endpoint depends on the token scope it describes.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on authentication.

Authentication uses a bearer token scoped to one account. Include the token in the Authorization header on every request. A token carries one or more scopes: `read` for listing and fetching bookings, `write` for creating, updating, and canceling them. Requests to collaborator calendars check the collaborator's own read or write permission on top of the token's scope, so a write-scoped token still cannot modify a calendar where its account has read-only access. Tokens do not expire on a fixed schedule; revoke one from the account settings endpoint when it is no longer needed.

output: Using a bearer token means putting a secret code in every request you send, so the API knows which account is asking. Get this token from your account settings, then include it in the Authorization header on every call. The token also determines what you can do: a read scope lets you list and look up bookings, a write scope lets you create, change, or cancel them. If a calendar belongs to someone else and they've added you as a collaborator, your access depends on what they granted you, read or write, even if your token itself has write access. Tokens stay valid until you revoke them. There's no automatic expiration, so if you stop using a token, revoke it from account settings rather than leaving it active.
